en: Regulations for the Seven-Day Period of Mindful Recitation of the Buddha’s Name with Single-Minded Diligence.
Compiled by the Bhikṣu Xingce of the Pure Practice Community at Puren Monastery on Mount Yu.
Rules and Procedures.
Select a pure and spacious mansion to serve as seven halls. In the central hall, enshrine a sacred image of Amitābha;
suspend various flowered banners, light lamps, and burn incense without interruption for seven days. Adorn the space solely with fragrance and light, making offerings according to the Dharma;
do not use fruits, vegetables, hymns, or musical instruments. On both the left and right sides within the hall, set out a long table each, also using incense burners and ritual implements.
Adorn and decorate [the area]. Outside the tables, set four chairs each. In the center, facing the Buddha, set one long table level with the left and right tables;
the two crosswise tables should be separated by about one or two feet so that passage for entry and exit is possible.

Upon the table, place one copy of the ritual text (*śāstra*), one large incense burner, and flower candles and offering implements, ensuring they are all proportionate. Outside the table, place a *pú-dūn* (cushion).
Four [seats] are placed near the walls on both sides. If there are no meditation platforms (*zanchuang*), many seating positions are provided so that one may withdraw and sit according to the ranks.
The accompanying pure companions are fixed at twelve persons, divided into three groups of four.

The first position in each group serves as the *siling* (bell-ringer), keeping track of the Buddha-recitation with a total of one thousand recitations as the standard. The next position serves as the *xiaoyu* (small fish-bell ringer). The final two positions...
The Inspector oversees the assembly. Those who appear drowsy or distracted within the ranks are to be cautioned. The central section facing the Buddha constitutes the first rank;
the person nearest the west serves as its head, who is also the leader of the seven. To the right, facing east, is the second rank;
the person nearest the top serves as its head. To the left, facing west, is the third rank; the person nearest the bottom serves as its head.

On the two long tables, one above and one below the Buddha image, place a pair of *yin-qing* (striking gongs) and small fish-shaped cymbals respectively; these should be returned to the tables as soon as they have been used.
For all seven halls of ritual arrangements, everything must be fully prepared the night before. Likewise, the seven monastics and laypeople must assemble together on the day prior.
After they have bathed, they should invite the Master of the Seven-Day Retreat (*zhushi*) in advance to assign the classes and designate their positions, providing instructions for the performance.

Practice: In each session, circumambulate the Buddha one hundred times, then return to your position to change shifts. During the circumambulation, strike the "great fish" bell six times to serve as a substitute for the meal gong.
After the three sessions have been conducted according to the Dharma, proceed to the refectory hall. While circumambulating there, chant as before;

stop the "fish" bell and take up the wooden clapper (*ban*), then join the clapper with the Buddha-recitation. Return to the hall, circumambulate, and sit down. Each of these instructions must be clearly explained so that the assembly understands them thoroughly.
All of this must be practiced in advance because the instructions for the precepts are given during the period [of retreat] and cannot be taught at that time. Once the practice is mastered,
each person should sincerely prostrate to the Buddha and pray for the Buddha’s empowerment so that the work may be completed within seven days and nights,
without the arising of internal or external demonic obstacles, and so that the task may be finished early to avoid exhaustion.

On the first day, at the fifth watch, the signal bell is struck. The assembly rises, and after completing their ablutions, they enter with hot water. The Hall Master and the seven masters strike the leading chime.

They perform three prostrations before the Buddha and each takes their place according to rank. The incense praise is recited, followed by the Amitābha Sūtra, the tone of which must be harmonious and slow.

The *Nianfo Shengwang Zhu* (Recitation of the Mantra for Rebirth) is recited three times, followed by verses in praise of the Buddha, after which the name of the Buddha is invoked. This is the middle section.
The *mingqing* is struck twice. After bowing and circumambulating, the assembly divides into left and right ranks, then sits upright and remains silent, following [the recitation] with their minds.

If those who are prone to dullness or distraction are heavy in these states, they should slightly move their lips and teeth; this will help avoid the interruption of "sitting-forgetfulness" (*zuowang*) and falling into the state of indeterminate nature (*wujixing*) characterized by torpor (*chenshen*).
Those whose spirit and breath are clear and bright should close their eyes and listen quietly, focusing the single mind on the Buddha, so that the Buddha within the heart...
The chanting is clear and resonant, like beads on a string—neither muddled nor interrupted. Once the first group has completed their circumambulation, they stand empty at the bottom edge;
then, upon the syllable *ta*, the lead chime is struck once. Thereupon, the second group rises from their seats and gracefully withdraws from their positions.
Standing in a single row beside the Buddha table, the head of the assembly strikes the leading chime once.

After four or five more strikes following the word "Buddha," he strikes it twice consecutively on the two characters for "Tathāgata" (Nyorai). He then ceases and performs a formal greeting before the Buddha, taking his seat in the vacant position to the right.

The next member of the assembly follows by performing a greeting before the Buddha and circumambulating as previously described. When the recitation of the Buddha’s name is finished, they return to their positions at the top.

Stand in meditation. After the third strike of the lead chime, the last row rises from their seats and leaves their positions; they proceed to the lower side to join the circumambulation of the Buddha, exactly as in the previous rite.
The next row then returns to sit in the vacant space on the left, silently following the recitation of the Buddha’s name.

In this manner, three rounds are completed and then begun again, continuing from dawn until dusk with the sound of the Buddha’s name never ceasing. Each time one thousand recitations are reached, they follow in silence.

Two thousand [prostrations] are performed while walking; one thousand are performed while circumambulating; two thousand are performed while sitting upright. This ensures that body and speech do not grow weary and that labor and rest are balanced.

When the circumambulation is completed, one should simply observe whether there are no small fish near the table; only then should one stand up. In this way, there will never be any discrepancy between the upper and lower sections.
Beyond the twelve people, regardless of the number of monastics or laypeople, they are also divided into three groups. When walking...
As for the seating arrangement: when sitting, one sits in a recessed position.
In the refectory, circular seats are arranged on three sides with long tables joined together; only the center of the lower side is slightly open to allow for passage through the hall.

The seats near the walls on all four sides permit circumambulation. (Although the layout follows the cardinal directions, it is called "circular" to signify the sense of revolving around the perimeter.)
Aside from the three daily meals of rice gruel and cooked rice, one additional meal is served before noon. Vegetables are limited to two vessels, shared by two people.

After each meal, once the distribution of food has concluded, the wooden sounding block is struck six times (signifying *Namo Amitābha Buddha*). Upon hearing the sound of the block in the hall, members of any class shall circumambulate as usual while reciting the name.
Upon reaching the side of the desk for the liturgical texts, the head of the class places the prayer beads upon the table.

The ritual chime strikes twice for the conclusion of the recitation. The monks inquire after one another’s well-being. (If the Buddha-recitation has been too rapid, at this point one should change to a slow, steady rhythm. The attendants on both sides rise to their feet.
They chant together in unison. The head of the assembly leads with the *jing* (hand chime) and proceeds along the central path to circumambulate the Buddha.
They likewise exit the hall by the central path. If the first group is at the front, the remaining two groups follow in succession;

they must wait until their own respective groups of monastics and laypeople have completely passed before the next group may join the procession. If the middle group happens to be at the front, then the last group follows, while the first group [remains behind].
The junior class shall remain behind. If the junior class is at the front, the senior class shall follow, with the next class remaining behind;

they must not overtake or disrupt the order. Upon reaching the refectory, they shall circumambulate it once to the right. Waiting until the last person has reached their place, the leader of the senior class shall strike the *yin-磬* (guiding gong) once, signaling the cessation of the *yu* (fish-shaped bell) and the stopping of the *fo* (Buddha-bell).
Monastics and laypeople shall take their seats according to their respective positions. One must not push forward or yield one's seat to others.
Afterwards, one must not withdraw from one’s seat. One should eat while seated and need not perform inquiries, recitations, or the *chusheng* (emergence) ritual.
A board and mallet set should be suspended nearby; a novice should be stationed at the side of the board beforehand to wait until the small fish have ceased moving.

Upon their stillness, he shall take up the board and chant the Buddha’s name, striking the board twice for each utterance. While the assembly eats, they should single-mindedly focus on the Buddha; they must not [be distracted].
Do not be negligent. When the meal is finished, the head of the assembly strikes the *yin-qing* bell once upon the character "Nan" (南).

The *śrāmaṇera* then strikes twice consecutively upon the characters "Duo Fo" (陀佛) to signal the closing of the wooden board (*jie-ban*). The assembly simultaneously leaves their seats; they do not exchange greetings.

They immediately rise, circumambulate the Buddha to the right, and return to the hall according to the previous order of seating. When the head of the assembly reaches his original standing place, he strikes the *yin-qing* bell.

The two [officiants] descend and inquire after [the Buddha’s] well-being, placing [the offerings] upon the table; they then take up their prayer beads and circumambulate the Buddha. The remaining rows return to their original seats.
Those in the left row facing west must proceed clockwise to the edge of the table, entering from the rear seat; they must not return directly, nor may they walk in reverse order.
Whenever returning to one's seat, leaving the assembly, or entering and exiting for any purpose, one must always move with composed and slow steps; one must not act otherwise.
They ran with staggering steps. As night fell and the sunlight first dimmed, the long candles were likewise placed upon the offering tables.

Thereafter, approximately every session, after completing two circumambulations and the recitation of the names of the Six Thousand Buddhas, they waited for the next session to join the Buddha-recitation procession.
The seven leaders emerge from their positions. The lead chime is struck once, and the assembly in the hall all rises.

They chant together in a circumambulatory recitation (*xuánniàn*), no longer observing the order of the three classes of monastics and laypeople. They simply perform about ten circumambulations while chanting. Afterwards, the seven leaders stand facing the Buddha at the center of the lower section.
The lead chime is struck three times to conclude with a "small fish" (*xiǎoyú*) sequence and bring the recitation to rest. The entire assembly then faces the Buddha.
Sound the chime. Together recite the Verse of Aspiration: "We, the assembly of disciples, make this aspiration with a sincere heart:

May our spirits remain undisturbed at the time of death; With right mindfulness, may we be reborn directly in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), To behold Amitābha face-to-face and encounter the multitude of sages, There to practice the ten stages and enjoy supreme, eternal bliss."
At the end of the final three characters, ring the chime slowly three times. Immediately perform three prostrations to the Buddha, return to your seat, and go to sleep.

At that time, you and the assembly should especially guard the three karmas; rest with right mindfulness, and must not engage in other activities, speak other words, or give rise to other miscellaneous thoughts.
Furthermore, you must not prostrate to other Buddhas, recite other sutras or mantras, even if you have regular daily recitations.
Those who have failed to maintain it without interruption throughout their entire lives should likewise cease [other practices] for seven days and subsequently make up for the deficiency.
Otherwise, one cannot avoid the faults of interruption and intermixture; how, then, could such practice be called "holding the Name with single-mindedness and without distraction" for seven days?
After resting and sleeping, when two sticks of official incense have nearly burned out, the incense-lamp master informs the kitchen in advance to prepare noodles, water, and hot soup.
Immediately, the announcement bell is struck. Following this, for six days, once entering the hall to pay homage to the Buddha, one immediately recites verses of praise for the Buddha;
no sutras or mantras are chanted. All other matters are conducted as on the first day. During the period of observance, seven masters are invited to provide fixed protection, with two serving as...
Regarding the external protection for the duration of the retreat: generally, those of both monastic and lay status who come out of sympathetic interest must not be allowed to enter the hall.

Only those who have come specifically to practice *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) shall be guided inside. Once they have performed three prostrations before the Buddha, they shall be sent to join the ranks for circumambulation and recitation, or sent to the rear of the left or right rows.
They must not bow to the assembly or converse with them. If one wishes to leave before the period is complete, one should likewise simply perform prostrations before the Buddha and depart.
One need not join the assembly of monastics and laypeople; rather, one should arrive in advance on the seventh day prior.
Those who have made a vow to complete the seven-day period must finish the entire course, as this differs from the practice of merely joining in sympathetic rejoicing (*anumodana*).

Should one be advanced in years or afflicted by illness such that one’s strength cannot sustain the journey, one may privately inform the master overseeing the seven-day retreat and request a written authorization to be conveyed to the presiding host. Thus, one may travel briefly and sit for short intervals, or even remain until nightfall.
Afterwards, at the early rest period, one should employ skillful means to break through [obstacles]. Next, appoint one *jianzhi* (supervisor) monk;

if anyone among the assembly violates the agreement, their name shall be recorded immediately and they shall be punished without fail. Next, assign one person for incense and lamps and two practitioners (*xingzhe*).

The incense and lamp attendants are responsible for the hearth, incense, and candles; whenever the candles grow dim, they must trim them, and whenever the incense is exhausted, they must replace it. The assembly...
When attending a meal, one must remain in the hall and not leave. When the assembly retires for the night, one must watch the incense and keep watch through the night;

this duty must be assigned to those who are mature and experienced. If one becomes fatigued, one should exchange duties with the *jianzhi* (supervisor of the night watch) to rest; however, one must never neglect the task or cause error among the assembly.
The attendant (xingzhe) shall manage matters such as serving tea and water for washing and bathing. Tea is served twice before noon;
after noon, there is no fixed number of servings; and once again at nightfall. After each service is completed, the vessels must be collected and rinsed immediately.

Once the assembly has returned to their seats for meditation, the services must be resumed. Whenever water from the basins is required for washing or by the community, the attendant must provide it with all due diligence.
Prepare the offerings. The masters presiding over the seven-day period must manage affairs according to the occasion and ensure that nothing is neglected or abandoned.
On the day the seven days are completed, after nightfall and the conclusion of the recitation of the Six Thousand Buddhas, wait further for the second shift to join in the reception of the Buddhas.

Thereafter, the master presiding over the seven-day period shall, as usual, sound the leading chime; the three classes of practitioners shall rise together and circumambulate while reciting the name of the Buddha five hundred times. The master presiding over the seven-day period [then proceeds] before the Buddha...

At the head of the eastern side of the hall, stand facing the Buddha. Ring the large chime once; the assembly shall all face the Buddha. When the third strike is sounded, follow it with a simultaneous tolling of the bell and drum.
Ring the "Great Fish" (mahāmatsya). Kneel and recite the names of Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the Pure Ocean Assembly ten times each, according to the procedure for the evening service.
Recite the Short Text on the Pure Land, perform the Dedication of Merit, and prostrate twelve times before the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas.
Perform three prostrations. Upon the completion of the three refuges, strike the large chime once. The assembly stands facing one another in a side-by-side position.

The seven masters of the rite proceed to the center of the lower section, where they arrange their ritual implements, prostrate before the Buddha, and kneel for a long duration. The assembly recites, "Namo to the Great Vehicle’s Ever-Abiding Triple Gem.

Once the seven masters of the rite have finished proclaiming the memorial text (*śāstra*), they again strike the small fish-shaped bell and chant the *Wǎngshēng Zhòu* (Rebirth Mantra) while escorting the text; there is no fixed limit to the number of rounds.

Having finished counting and reciting the dhāraṇī, one recites the verses of aspiration and offers greetings. Returning before the Buddha, the assembly together spreads their sitting cloths and performs three prostrations.
They withdraw the cloths, offer greetings, and the lead chime is struck to lead the assembly out of the hall. They proceed to the quarters of the Seven Masters of the Retreat to offer thanks.

The Seven Masters, together with the assembly, go to the place of the Master of the Seven-day Protection and the places of the various office-holding masters, visiting the various dormitories in order to exchange greetings.
Having finished the expressions of thanks, they then return to the hall for the full prostrations, marking the conclusion of the session.

Regarding the regulations for penalties, there are three grades: the upper penalty is one hundred coins, the middle is fifty coins, and the lower is ten coins; these are applied regardless of [the specific offense].
The value of the money shall be determined according to this standard as a model. A water-board shall be suspended within the hall, upon which a set of brush and inkstone is placed.
Should there be one who merits a fine, the supervisor on duty shall immediately record it upon the board. Once recorded, he shall present it to the individual concerned so that they may take notice;

when the period expires, the total amount of the fine for [Name] shall be settled, and the individual shall further be required to purchase incense to offer to the Buddha, or to release [a living being].
Life. For those who lack funds, they shall be penalized by being required to recite the *Wǎngshēng Zhòu* (Sūtra for Rebirth). Ten recitations of the mantra shall be equivalent to one coin.
During this period, first of all, speech is strictly prohibited, whether inside or outside the hall.

From the time before the Buddha has risen until after the Buddha has retired, anyone who violates this incurs one penalty; upon the third offense, the offender shall be expelled from the hall. Should there be unavoidable circumstances, [the following applies].

If you must speak, you may whisper it secretly to the Seven Teachers of Protection; speak only one or two words and then stop. If you speak at length or in a loud voice, the penalty shall be the same.
Whenever you have finished tasks such as relieving yourself or dressing, rise up and return quickly once your business is concluded; do not linger outside under the pretext of some task.

Regarding those who are lax: for a minor offense, one receives the lower penalty. If one enters a dormitory privately and sits or lies down there even for a brief moment, one receives the upper penalty.
When wishing to leave the hall on business, person A must come out first and person B may go out afterward; if A has not yet returned, B must wait a short while.
However, if the matter is urgent, it is permissible for two people to exit simultaneously. If, among four people, two have already exited and the third person...
Regarding those who leave again: first, as for those who have been punished, they may leave at will and sit behind their respective ranks; this is not restricted.
However, while the circumambulation has not yet concluded, one must not leave the ranks to exit. One must wait until everyone has returned to their seats and is settled before one may withdraw.
If anyone bypasses their rank to exit, both monastics and laypeople shall receive the same intermediate punishment.
When the upper ranks have nearly finished circumambulating the Buddha, those in the lower ranks must not leave their positions.
If one leaves the hall at an improper time and consequently fails to attend their assigned rank, they shall receive one intermediate punishment.
When the monastics and laypeople proceed in their respective ranks during circumambulation, unless one is elderly or ill and has formally requested to sit in front, one must not sit down arbitrarily;
those who do so shall be penalized with one *xià* (a prostration).
If, while others are sitting peacefully, one who is constitutionally unable to sit joins another rank to perform circumambulatory recitation, one shall be penalized with one *zhōng* (a light bow).
Those who repeatedly enter and exit shall be punished with one demerit point, except in cases of illness.

When leaving the row to return to one's place, as well as when exiting or entering the hall, one must maintain dignified and orderly deportment; those who stumble or act with haste and urgency shall be punished.
One strike as punishment for moving about within the hall. One strike as punishment for those who obstruct the assembly by turning left.
One strike as punishment for those who cut through the ranks to enter or exit.

If the incense and lamp master is not present in the hall and the candles grow dim or the incense is exhausted, the first and last members of the left and right ranks, or those seated in the rear rows, may all temporarily rise to act on his behalf.
However, when circumambulating, neither monastics nor laypeople shall trim the candles or add more incense.
Standing still obstructs those who follow behind. Any who violate this shall be penalized with one prostration.
Among the three classes of monastics and laypeople, should there be any who act improperly like fish, they must recite silently or in a low voice when approaching their ranks.

If one raises their voice and disturbs the assembly, they shall receive one stroke of punishment. The Seven Protectors (Saptācāryas) shall lead them to a secluded place and privately inform them [of the offense].

At night, they must stop by the Buddha’s seat and sleep according to the assembly. If they wish to further prostrate before the Buddha, perform recitations, or engage in other meritorious practices, they may do so.

In such cases, there shall be one middle penalty. The incense and lamp master (*xiāngdēngshī*) should exhort them to desist; if they do not listen, he shall then inform the supervisor on duty (*jiānzhíshī*), who shall record the penalty.
When proceeding to the refectory for meals, if the two ranks of attendants lose their order of precedence, the heads of each rank shall receive one middle penalty.
If, after finishing the meal in the Zhai Hall, one rises to relieve oneself and commits even a single instance of this, they shall be penalized.

Furthermore, if one fails to settle for the night at the appointed time and consequently enters the hall late, such that the three classes of practitioners have already completed less than one full cycle of recitation by the break of dawn, they shall likewise be penalized.

The incense and lamp master shall receive one lower penalty for failing to enter the hall promptly. He shall receive one upper penalty for falling asleep or losing track of the incense, or for entering too early and causing the assembly to become weary.
He shall receive one middle penalty for similar lapses.
The supervising officers on duty shall, at all times and in all places, diligently inspect for the sake of the community and record [infractions] according to the prescribed form.
If they repeatedly fail to recognize an offense, or though recognizing it fail to record it, they shall be punished in the same manner as the individual offender.
In general, for all seven types of protection and the seven masters, one must thoroughly master the regulations prior to their implementation.

Next, the examples of penalties shall be transcribed and posted before the guest hall. Should any monastics or laypeople arrive later, they must first be required to carefully examine the articles of agreement before being admitted into the hall.
If they do not understand the meaning of the text, an abstract of the essential points must be explained to them. If they are hastily led in, it will result in...
Entering the Hall: For those who are ignorant and repeatedly violate the regulations, the Seven Teachers shall impose a punishment of one unit.
These three grades of punishment comprise twenty-three articles in total. Now, the specific forms for recording these punishments are clarified as follows.
Violating the prohibition against speaking: one level of penalty.
Speaking excessively: one level of penalty.
Speaking in a loud voice: one level of penalty.
Entering the dormitory to sit or lie down: one upper penalty.
Failing to observe the fixed hours of the night: one upper penalty.
Leaving the hall out of order: one middle penalty.
Leaving the hall at an improper time: one medium penalty.
Disturbing the order of the assembly while reciting: one medium penalty.
Performing spiritual practices separately after nightfall: one medium penalty.
If one misses their place in the assembly, there is one medium penalty.
If one fails to attend during the fixed night session, there is one medium penalty.
If one leaves for a long time on some pretext, there is one minor penalty.
Leaving the hall one after another: one penalty.
Sitting or standing in the ranks out of turn: one penalty.
Entering and exiting repeatedly: one penalty.
Moving with undue haste: one penalty.
Turning left against the group: one penalty.
Rushing through the ranks to enter or exit: one penalty.
Standing still and obstructing those behind: one penalty.
Speaking loudly and disturbing the assembly: one penalty.
Rising before the meal is finished: one penalty.
To allow someone to enter the hall in haste: one penalty.
To lose the appointed time for the night vigil: one penalty.

As stipulated in the regulations above, these matters must be strictly enforced. This is intended to restrain negligence and assist in the accomplishment of superior practice; it is not done out of a desire for [punishment].

This would be overly burdensome and restrictive. Practitioners should reflect that a single lifetime passes in an instant; they must exert themselves with fierce determination for these seven days alone, not sparing even their own lives.

Whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, eating, drinking, or attending to the calls of nature, the single great name must be recited like breathing—without interruption, never ceasing for even a moment.
If one allows it to be mixed with other thoughts for even an instant, since one desires...
"One mind, undistracted. This is vastly different from ordinary forms of *nien-fo*; reflect upon it and exert yourself! The Preface (to be written on the cover:

"Preface for the Dedication of Merit and Vows for the Seven-Day *Nien-fo* Retreat. Submitted by the seven *śramaṇas* [names] who uphold the teachings and cultivate the Pure Land, sealed with their seals).
We humbly observe that when the one mind is perfectly pure, one does not depart from the five turbidities yet dwells in the land of serene peace; one transcends the three realms horizontally.

Though there are nine grades, how could they be separated from the ranks of the common and ordinary? He merges the supreme Samādhirāja within the ocean of nature and turns the wheel of the primary truth with his mouth.
The Way is propagated by men; the Buddha responds according to capacities.

The bhikṣus, so-and-so by name, of such-and-such monastery in such-and-such district, prefecture, and province of the Great Qing Empire, having bathed themselves this very day, prostrate with sincere devotion and take refuge in the Teacher of the Sahā World, our Original Master Śākyamuni Buddha;
in Amitābha Buddha, the Guide who receives us in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; and in Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and all the holy sages. May you all together bestow your compassion.
With compassion, please deign to grant your witness and discernment. I, the disciple [Name], together with all sentient beings present before me, have been born into this age of turbidity;

our retribution is that of ordinary bodies. Though we have committed no transgression among the three karmas and six sense faculties, we have experienced every suffering within the five destinies and eight difficulties.
Ignorance has been transmitted through successive lifetimes without ever awakening; as birth and death stretch out vast and boundless, where is there liberation?

I pray that, having fortunately planted slight causes in past lives, I may attain right faith, enter early into the ocean of Amitābha’s vows, and exclusively cultivate the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land.
May I pray for the precious realm to be my dwelling for the spirit and entrust my thoughts to the lotus wheel upon my passing.

To this end, I rely on the sutras to establish the ritual procedures and accord with the teachings to honor this cultivation. Beginning from the [day] of this month, I respectfully initiate the practice of single-minded, diligent mindfulness.

In the Buddha’s place of enlightenment, for seven consecutive days, they solemnly adorned the hall and its ritual implements. They maintained their respective ranks with gravity, upheld the sacred names, and did not deviate from these practices throughout the mealtime.
They kept the Great Name in mind, never departing from it for even a moment. By means of this merit, they dedicated it toward rebirth in the Pure Land.
I pray that Amitābha Buddha, out of his great compassion, will graciously accept me; together with the assembly of holy ones, may he personally descend to guide and lead me.
May my faculties be brought to stillness and right mindfulness be made manifest. May the realm of *Sukhāvatī* appear before my eyes, and may golden lotuses bloom as I relinquish this life.
As stated in the sutras, may all these vows be fulfilled without fail. Furthermore, I pray that by the merit of these seven days of diligent practice, [may I attain rebirth in the Pure Land].

May all these beings universally sever the sevenfold evils, extinguish the seven obstructing offenses, eliminate the hindrances of the seven types of pride, and depart from the seven defiled practices.

May they roam the pools of the seven jewels, spread the flowers of the seven purities, possess the wisdom and eloquence of the sevenfold discrimination, expound the seven factors of enlightenment, transcend the stages of the seven expedient means, and realize the fruit of the sevenfold eternal abiding.
Furthermore, I vow that by means of these three classes of pure companions, this assembly of twelve monks—
Through the merit produced by practicing in harmony, may all beings universally sever the three evil paths, transform the three heavy obstructions, purify the three clusters of precepts,
traverse the stages of the three vehicles, gallop far beyond the three realms, and ascend loftily above the three ranks of practitioners.
They enter deeply into the three gates of liberation and fully manifest the three Tathāgatagarbhas.

Furthermore, they vow that once all beings have attained Buddhahood, they shall sit beneath the Bodhi tree, contemplate for twenty-one days, and for the sake of all sentient beings, preach the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.

They shall turn the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Noble Truths in its twelve aspects, extensively explaining the twelve links of dependent origination across the three periods of time—both their forward progression and their reverse cessation.
This Dharma gate ultimately leads all to the same ocean of *sarvajñā* (omniscience).

Furthermore, I vow that during these seven days, whether they be monastics or laypeople, those far or near, those staying long or for a short time, those coming or going—even those who perform manual labor and exert physical strength—[may all attain this].
May all who see or hear [this teaching] rejoice; may they all emerge from the wheel of suffering and together be born in the Land of Bliss.
May they behold the ūrṇā-kośa mark on the brow of Sumeru and gaze together upon the Dharmadhātu-garbha body.

Furthermore, I vow that once the assembly has attained rebirth in Sukhāvatī and drawn near to Amitābha, they shall serve all Tathāgatas, travel to adorn all Buddha-fields, and encounter all spiritual friends.
May we be able to accord with all things; may we attain thorough penetration into all Dharma-gates; may all sentient beings receive our deliverance;
and may all our practices and vows be fully accomplished. Though space may come to an end, my vows shall be inexhaustible.
I respectfully pray that the Triple Gem bear witness and grant that we may obtain what we have prayed for, fulfilling our bodhi-vows.
Record of the Universal Benevolence’s Seven-Day Buddha-Recitation (Appendix).
By Jin Shanding.

In the spring of the Jindin year, at the Puren Chan Monastery north of Yushan, on the occasion of the Great Being’s birthday, [this was performed] in accordance with the teachings of the *Amitābha Sūtra*.
He established the new regulation for seven days of Buddha-recollection (*buddhānusmṛti*). Thereupon, he gathered a pure assembly, making no distinction between monastics and laity.
Its presiding master was the Great Master Puren, known as the Wayman Jieliu; its external protectors were the masters Shenyue and Siguna;
and its fellow practitioners among the black-robed clergy were Yuehai, Zaijian, Huiri, Zhan, Yuezhi, Cihong, Haimu, and De.
Yongyue reverently esteemed the Dharma and was worthy of being honored once again.
Those who heard of the Dharma from afar and came by boat were the two monks from Loushan, Minggu and Dinghui. Among the lay practitioners (upāsakas) were the elder Wang Lüsan, Mr.
Fengrui Gu, Jin Shuiren, Chen Qianqing, the elder Zhao Cunhu, the elder Weng Ziyu, Kang Cheng Shen, and Danxian.
The summer is the period of constancy. Reciting the Buddha’s name is the shortcut to rebirth in the Pure Land, and Avalokiteśvara is the guide of the Western Paradise;
therefore, the date chosen is the nineteenth day of the second month. As for the ritual: twelve monks are selected and divided into three shifts, with four monks in each shift.
Each has its assigned duty. Beyond the twelve officials, regardless of whether they are monastics or laypeople, or their numbers, they are likewise divided into three groups.
As one group proceeds to circumambulate, the other two groups sit at ease. When it is time for the meal, they proceed to the refectory in order, with no daring to disrupt the sequence.
Once everyone was seated and the Buddha’s voice had just ceased, the junior *śrāmaṇera* struck the wooden board, followed by the chanting of the Buddha’s name.

This ensured that the single great name (*ekākṣara-nāmadheya*) would not cease from the heart, the mouth, or the ears. They slept briefly during the middle watch of the night; upon hearing the bell toll, they rose together. Those who walked to the left were penalized;
those who overstepped their positions were penalized; and those who conversed with one another were doubly penalized. Thus, it was as strict as military discipline. On this day...

Ye Wangxuan and several others were already present when I arrived later. I heard the sound of the Buddha’s name resonating clearly from within the hall. A ritual master guarding the altar led me inside;
we were permitted only to prostrate before the Buddha and were not allowed to bow to the assembly. We simply followed the ranks as they moved, and subsequently withdrew to sit.
Some silently followed the chanting of the Buddha’s name with their lips slightly moving, while others closed their eyes to listen quietly, following it with their minds. The rest...
Those who arrive later should do likewise. The sound of reciting the Buddha’s name should at times be gentle and resonant, like a single breath, continuous and unbroken.
When the sound becomes vigorous and rapid, it should be like a fierce general pursuing an enemy, not ceasing until the task is complete.
This ensures that no interval remains for delusive thoughts to enter and leaves no path for the various demons to invade. When the wind [of mindfulness] is thus...

When rain fell and the world was shrouded in darkness, the myriad sounds vibrated and resounded; one could no longer discern that mist was rising from the mountain peaks or that the halls and pavilions were sealed by clouds.
When the sky brightened and the air cleared, the pines sighed with the wind and the mountain streams murmured—there was nothing that did not harmonize with the sound of reciting the Buddha’s name.
As for the time when the roosters crowed at dawn, the lamps flickered dimly, the morning sun was just beginning to rise, and the incense smoke curled in spirals.
At dawn, one recites the Buddha’s name. The mountain light suddenly fades; the forests and valleys grow dark and secluded. All sounds fall silent, and the sound of the Dharma alone rises.

At dusk, one recites the Buddha’s name. Perhaps the spirit and mind are serene and joyful, untainted by a single speck of dust, with only the four characters remaining—this is truly one who can maintain single-mindedness without distraction.
Or perhaps, with a sudden surge of vigor, the spirit seems to gallop forth.
The mind desires to come to rest; this depends upon the single-mindedness of not allowing distraction.

Yet, if one is unable to achieve this—despite having already established firm faith and aspiration, and having encountered excellent conditions—then worldly affairs will press heavily and demonic obstacles will arise in manifold ways, causing one to rely on the practice for a brief moment only to depart from that state once again.

I sigh with deep regret that I have not been able to complete these seven days. Our Great Master’s skillful means for delivering sentient beings were profound, and his compassionate instructions were most sincere.
We all believe that the Western Land can indeed be reached, and we have fortunately followed him day and night. Knowing that his great name is inconceivable, our tears flow as we extol it.
Alas! Like a spark from a flint or a flash of lightning, the hundred years of human life are but like these seven days.
A day and seven days are used to attend to worldly burdens; yet when will these burdens ever end? A day and seven days are used to seek the Pure Land;

yet the Pure Land can certainly be expected. Moreover, within a hundred years, those seven days are exceedingly many, whereas a single kṣaṇa constitutes an entirely different world, making those hundred years likewise extremely brief.
People know that a hundred years cannot be relied upon, yet they do not [realize this regarding the present moment].
One knows that these seven days are difficult to encounter, and one further realizes that a hundred years are spent in vain;
yet one does not realize that those seven days are being wasted. How tragic!
At Puren Temple in Changshu, after the Great Master Jieliu had turned his head toward the afterlife, Hanchen—the elder son of Mr.
Fusang, the Grand Secretary Sun Zhuangyuan—was summoned by the underworld authorities and passed away. After one day and one night, he revived and spoke, saying:
"While I was being detained in the darkness before the Lord of Yama, I suddenly beheld a radiance that illuminated the heavens, accompanied by fragrant flowers."
He spread out a cloth on the ground. Lord Yan prostrated himself on the earth and welcomed the Great Master from the West; upon examining him, it was indeed Lord Gong.
Because I was illuminated by the Master’s radiance, I was subsequently permitted to return home. On the same day, there was a son of the Wu family outside the southern gate.
He died and was revived after midnight. His account of what he had seen was also consistent with the words of Sunzi.
This is recorded by Shu Cheng-weng Shu Yuan Baolin on the first day of the full moon in the first month of the thirty-sixth year of the Kangxi era.
